chapters.title: Begin with a function map
chapters.text: Look over districts for compute, memory control and input/output. Chiplets partition a system into integrable dies; placing arbitrary chips together does not make them cooperate. First map which functions exchange which data, then decide where splitting the system is worthwhile.

chapters.title: Match process to function
chapters.text: Different functions need not use the same process technology. Partitioning can match technology to purpose, but adds interface, power and packaging costs. Chiplets are a design option, not a requirement for every product; a smaller, simpler system may favor another architecture.

chapters.title: UCIe defines interface rules
chapters.text: At the die boundary, UCIe supplies standardized rules for on-package die-to-die connectivity, including physical and communication mechanisms. It is not a silicon bridge or a cooling technology. Separate the package structure from the interconnect standard before combining them into a system.

chapters.title: Co-design before assembly
chapters.text: Before placing dies, align interface locations, power requirements, clocking strategy and package capability. Standardization can reduce coordination work, but cannot automatically solve every compatibility issue. The assembly animation represents designed integration, not a guarantee that any two components are plug-and-play.

chapters.title: Physical layer and protocol
chapters.text: The section reveals metal and contacts; the upper view shows messages. Physical connectivity addresses reliable signaling, while protocols organize the meaning and management of data. Similar-looking connections need not carry identical semantics. Verify what functions both endpoints actually support.

chapters.title: Communication has a cost
chapters.text: Follow data between functional districts. Every boundary crossing requires interface work; excessive partitioning can add communication and synchronization overhead. The roadmap must budget data volume, latency and energy instead of merely adding up the computing capability of individual blocks.

chapters.title: A hotspot affects its neighbors
chapters.text: Switch the function map to an illustrative heat map. Observe the distance between a busy die and its neighbors. System performance may be limited by the hottest die, weakest power path or busiest link. Coordinate power management and cooling rather than treating dies as isolated islands.

chapters.title: Compatibility needs evidence
chapters.text: Test not only whether dies work separately, but whether the assembled system meets shared conditions. Exercise link startup, error handling and target workloads; record versions and configurations. A UCIe label does not replace complete product-level integration and interoperability validation.

chapters.title: Reuse and integration effort
chapters.text: Reusing chiplets can make product families more flexible, while adding supplier, version and validation coordination. Compare monolithic and chiplet designs using development time, cost per good unit and long-term maintenance. No partition fits every need; preserve the reasoning behind each architectural trade-off.

chapters.title: Reconnect the system
chapters.text: Survey partitioning, interface selection, physical packaging, power, cooling and system validation. Distinguish three questions: what each die does, how the package connects it and how protocols coordinate behavior. Chiplet elegance comes from orderly specialization, supported by evidence that the whole system works.
